# Presentations {#sec-presentations}

This module is assessed with a short presentation in a lab session. The task is to communicate a finding to people who hear it once, at the pace set by the speaker.

The principles from @sec-writing-reports still apply: lead with the answer, give each chart one job and state the limits. A presentation needs more signposting because the audience cannot turn back a page.

## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

::: {.objectives}
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

1. Structure a short talk so the question and answer arrive early.
2. Build slides that support speech rather than duplicate it.
3. Explain a chart in the order a listener needs.
4. Rehearse a presentation against a fixed time limit.
5. Answer a question honestly when the available analysis does not settle it.
:::

## The Audience Gets One Pass {#sec-one-pass}

A reader who loses the thread can return to the previous paragraph. A listener has to keep moving.

Repeat the main finding. Use fewer numbers than a written report. Pause after introducing a chart and give the audience time to orient itself before explaining the pattern.

Signposting helps: "The question is...", "The main result is...", and "This chart provides the evidence..." These sentences may feel explicit to the speaker; they make the talk easier to follow.

## Structure a Short Talk {#sec-talk-structure}

For a five- to ten-minute presentation, use this sequence:

1. **Question:** What did the analysis investigate, and why does it matter?
2. **Answer:** State the main finding in one sentence.
3. **Evidence:** Use two or three charts or compact tables, each supporting one part of the answer.
4. **Limits:** Identify the uncertainty or missing information most relevant to the conclusion.
5. **Answer again:** End with the finding and its practical meaning.

Do not save the result for the final slide. An audience that knows the destination can follow the evidence; an audience waiting for the point has to guess how each detail fits.

The ending repeats the answer because it is the last complete idea the audience hears. "Any questions?" should invite discussion, not replace the conclusion.

## Build Slides for Listening {#sec-slides}

A slide should carry the visual evidence and a short statement of its meaning. It should not contain the script being spoken.

- **Use a claim as the headline.** "Canola yields were 15% higher in the black soil zone" tells the audience why the slide exists. "Yield by soil zone" only labels the topic.
- **Use one idea per slide.** Split a slide when its explanation requires "and separately" or a second conclusion.
- **Keep text short.** Use enough words to anchor the argument, not enough to compete with the speaker.
- **Make every element readable from the back of the room.** Test the projected size, not only the laptop view.
- **Enlarge charts.** Remove fine detail, small annotations and unnecessary series.
- **Keep the design consistent.** Headlines, fonts, colours and source notes should appear in the same places.

Six or seven slides are usually enough for a ten-minute talk. The exact count matters less than whether each slide receives enough time to be understood.

## Explain a Chart Out Loud {#sec-presenting-charts}

The presenter has studied the chart; the audience has just seen it. Explain it in this order:

1. **Axes:** "Yield in bushels per acre is on the vertical axis, and year is across the bottom."
2. **Marks:** "Each line represents one soil zone."
3. **Pattern:** "The black zone remains above the brown zone in all five years."
4. **Meaning:** "The yield gap therefore appears broader than one unusual season."

Point to the relevant line, bar or period while describing it. Then pause. Moving immediately to the next slide removes the audience's chance to inspect the evidence.

Do not read every value. Quote the one or two numbers needed to establish the scale of the result.

## Rehearse the Talk {#sec-presentation-rehearsal}

Rehearsal reveals problems that slide editing does not: a missing transition, a chart that takes too long to explain or a conclusion that arrives after the time limit.

Run the presentation from beginning to end with a timer. Speak at the intended pace and advance the actual slides. If it is too long, remove material rather than accelerating through it.

Check three times:

- once for structure and timing;
- once for chart explanations and transitions;
- once in the room or display setup, if possible, to check text size and colours.

The goal is not memorization. Know the opening, the main sentence for each slide and the final sentence. The connecting words can remain natural.

## Questions {#sec-talk-questions}

A question may go beyond the available data. Say so directly, identify what would be needed to answer it and stop there.

> I did not test whether the zones differ in seeding date. We would need field-level planting dates before separating that explanation from the soil-zone difference.

This is stronger than guessing. It distinguishes what the analysis shows from what remains possible.

If a question is unclear, ask the person to repeat or rephrase it. If the question identifies a real problem, acknowledge it and explain how it changes the conclusion.

## What Is Being Assessed {#sec-presentation-assessment}

The presentation is short and low-stakes. The assessment asks whether:

- the question and answer are clear within the first minute;
- the charts are readable and explained rather than merely displayed;
- quoted numbers can be traced to the analysis;
- limitations are stated honestly;
- the talk finishes within its assigned time.

Nervousness is not an analytical error. A talk succeeds when the audience can state what was found and why the evidence supports it.

## Other resources -- presenting

- **Michael Alley**, [The Craft of Scientific Presentations](https://www.craftofscientificpresentations.com/) -- the assertion-evidence approach, in which a slide headline makes a claim and the visual supports it.
- **Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic**, [Storytelling with Data](https://www.storytellingwithdata.com/blog) -- examples of reducing visual clutter and directing attention.
:::
